overview: A branch in Git is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. Creating one does not copy your files - it just writes a new label that points at a commit, so branching is nearly instant and costs almost nothing.

Branches let engineers work in isolation: you develop a new dbt model, Airflow DAG, or SQL transformation on a feature branch without touching the stable main branch that gets deployed, then combine your work back with a merge.

Merging integrates one branch's history into another. Sometimes Git can just slide the pointer forward (fast-forward); sometimes it has to build a merge commit that has two parents; and when both branches changed the same lines, you get a merge conflict that you resolve by hand before finishing the merge.
learningObjectives: Explain what a branch and HEAD are, and create, switch, list, and delete branches with git branch and git switch/checkout -b.
Merge one branch into another and distinguish a fast-forward merge from a three-way merge that creates a merge commit with two parents.
Recognise why merge conflicts happen, read the conflict markers, and resolve a conflict by editing, git add, and committing - or back out safely with git merge --abort.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A branch in Git is a named, movable reference (a pointer) to a single commit; because every commit records its parent(s), that one pointer implicitly names an entire line of history. HEAD is a special pointer to the branch (or commit) you currently have checked out, so the working directory reflects wherever HEAD points. The default branch (conventionally main, historically master) is simply the branch a repository starts on. Merging combines the histories of two branches: a fast-forward merge occurs when the target branch has not diverged, so Git just moves its pointer forward to the source commit with no new commit; a three-way merge occurs when both branches have new commits, so Git computes a new merge commit with two parents using the two branch tips and their common ancestor (the merge base). A merge conflict arises when the two sides make incompatible edits to the same region of a file; Git pauses the merge, writes conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into the affected files, and waits for you to resolve them, stage the result with git add, and complete the merge. Rebasing is an alternative that replays your commits on top of another branch to produce a linear history instead of a merge commit.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine your project's history is a single line of dominoes, each domino a commit. A branch is just a sticky note with a name on it, stuck to one domino - it says 'this is where this line of work is.' 'main' is the sticky note on the trusted, deployable line everyone relies on. When you want to try something risky - a new pipeline transformation - you put down a second sticky note called 'feature' on the same domino and start adding dominoes only that note points to. main stays untouched and safe. When your feature works, you 'merge': you tell Git to bring the feature dominoes into main. If main hasn't moved, Git just slides the main sticky note forward to catch up (fast-forward) - no new domino needed. If main did move (a teammate added dominoes too), Git has to build one special joining domino that connects both lines (a merge commit). The trouble comes when you and your teammate both scribbled on the same spot of the same file: Git can't guess who is right, so it stops and marks the file with <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> so you can look at both versions, decide what the final text should be, and tell Git you've sorted it out.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage Linux kernel development after the project lost access to its previous tool, BitKeeper. A defining design decision was to make branching and merging cheap and fast - unlike older centralized systems (CVS, Subversion) where a branch was an expensive server-side copy and merges were painful. In Git, a branch is just a 41-byte file containing a commit hash, so creating one is instant; this made branch-per-feature workflows practical. Around this design grew formal branching strategies: Vincent Driessen's 'GitFlow' (2010) with long-lived develop and release branches, GitHub's simpler 'GitHub Flow' built around short-lived feature branches and pull requests, and 'trunk-based development' favoured by high-throughput teams that merge tiny changes into main constantly. The default branch name changed from 'master' to 'main' across GitHub, GitLab, and Git itself around 2020. Today, branching and merging underpin virtually all collaborative software and data engineering: teams develop dbt models, Airflow DAGs, and infrastructure code on feature branches, review them via pull requests, and merge into a main branch that CI/CD deploys.

whyItMatters.business: Branches let a data team ship features and fixes in parallel without destabilising the pipelines the business depends on; main stays deployable while risky work happens elsewhere, so a broken experiment never takes down production dashboards or delays a release.
whyItMatters.engineering: Isolating work on branches means an engineer can iterate on a new transformation, throw it away or reshape it, and only integrate when it is ready and reviewed - and merging plus conflict resolution is the daily mechanic for combining many engineers' changes into one coherent codebase.
whyItMatters.scalability: Dozens of engineers can work on the same repository at once because each has their own branch; merging (with pull-request review) is what lets that parallel work converge safely instead of everyone editing one shared copy and clobbering each other.
whyItMatters.cost: Cheap branching avoids the wasted effort of maintaining separate copies of a repo or coordinating edits manually; catching conflicts and bad changes on a branch during review is far cheaper than discovering them in a deployed pipeline that has corrupted downstream data.
whyItMatters.reliability: Keeping main always in a known-good, deployable state - by only merging reviewed, tested branches - means the code that runs your production DAGs and models is trustworthy, and you can trace exactly which merge introduced a change when something breaks.

coreComponents.name: Branch (a movable pointer) and HEAD
coreComponents.definition: A branch is a named reference that points to one commit; because commits link to their parents, that pointer names a whole line of history. HEAD is the pointer to the branch you currently have checked out.
coreComponents.purpose: To label independent lines of work cheaply and to track where 'you are' so new commits attach to the right branch.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Advance automatically to the new commit each time you commit on that branch; let you list branches, create them, and move HEAD between them. main is just the conventional default branch that stays deployable.
coreComponents.examples: git branch (list) | git branch feature/new-model (create) | git switch main (move HEAD) | cat .git/HEAD (see where HEAD points)

coreComponents.name: Creating and switching branches (git branch, git switch/checkout)
coreComponents.definition: Commands that create a new branch pointer and move HEAD onto a branch so your working directory reflects it; git switch -c (or the older checkout -b) does both in one step.
coreComponents.purpose: To start isolated work off a known commit and to move between lines of work without copying files.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Create a branch at the current commit, check it out so new commits land there, list local and remote branches, and delete a branch pointer once its work is merged.
coreComponents.examples: git switch -c feature/add-dag | git checkout -b bugfix/null-key | git switch main | git branch -d feature/add-dag (delete merged)

coreComponents.name: Merging (git merge: fast-forward and three-way)
coreComponents.definition: Combining another branch's commits into the branch you are on. A fast-forward just moves the current branch pointer forward; a three-way merge creates a new merge commit with two parents when both branches have diverged.
coreComponents.purpose: To integrate completed work from a feature branch back into main (or to pull main's latest changes into your feature branch).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Find the common ancestor (merge base), combine changes, either advance the pointer (fast-forward) or build a merge commit, and stop and flag conflicts when the two sides changed the same lines.
coreComponents.examples: git merge feature/add-dag | git merge --no-ff feature/add-dag (always make a merge commit) | git merge --abort (back out)

coreComponents.name: Merge conflicts and their resolution
coreComponents.definition: A conflict occurs when both branches edit the same region of a file so Git cannot merge automatically; it writes conflict markers into the file and pauses. Resolution is editing to the desired final text, staging, and committing.
coreComponents.purpose: To let a human decide the correct combined content when two changes overlap, since Git will not silently guess and discard someone's work.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Mark conflicting regions with <<<<<<< HEAD / ======= / >>>>>>> branch, list conflicted files in git status, and require git add on each resolved file before git commit (or git merge --continue) finishes the merge.
coreComponents.examples: git status (see 'both modified') | edit file to remove markers | git add pipeline.yml | git commit | git merge --abort

internalWorking: Every commit is a snapshot identified by a SHA-1/SHA-256 hash that records its parent commit(s), forming a chain (a directed acyclic graph). A branch is nothing more than a tiny file under .git/refs/heads/ containing the hash of the commit at its tip - that is why creating a branch is instant and costs almost no space.

HEAD (the file .git/HEAD) normally holds a symbolic reference like 'ref: refs/heads/main', meaning 'I am on the main branch.' When you commit, Git creates the new commit object, then rewrites the current branch's ref file to point at the new commit, so the branch pointer moves forward automatically and HEAD follows it.

A fast-forward merge happens when the branch you are on is a direct ancestor of the branch being merged in (main has no new commits of its own). There is nothing to reconcile, so Git simply overwrites main's ref to point at the feature branch's tip - no merge commit is created and history stays linear.

A three-way merge happens when both branches have new commits since they diverged. Git finds their common ancestor (the merge base) and compares three snapshots - the base, your tip, and their tip - applying each side's changes. It then writes a new merge commit whose two parents are the two branch tips, joining the histories.

During a three-way merge, if the two sides changed the same lines relative to the base, Git cannot decide automatically. It writes the file with conflict markers (your version between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======, theirs between ======= and >>>>>>> branchname), records a MERGE_HEAD state so it knows a merge is in progress, and pauses. Once you edit the file, remove the markers, and 'git add' it, Git treats the conflict as resolved; 'git commit' (or 'git merge --continue') then writes the merge commit, while 'git merge --abort' restores the pre-merge state.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Start on main (HEAD -> main) -> git switch -c feature (new pointer at same commit) -> make commits (feature pointer advances, main unchanged) -> git switch main -> git merge feature -> Git finds merge base -> fast-forward (move main pointer) OR three-way merge (build merge commit with two parents) -> if same lines changed on both sides: CONFLICT, markers written, merge pauses -> edit to resolve, git add, git commit / --continue -> git branch -d feature
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You are on the stable main branch of the analytics repo, which CI deploys to production. To add a new revenue transformation without risking main, you create and switch to a feature branch: 'git switch -c feature/revenue-model'. Git writes a new ref pointing at main's current commit; no files are copied.

2. You edit models/revenue.sql and commit a few times. Each commit advances the feature/revenue-model pointer; main's pointer has not moved, so production is untouched. 'git log --graph --oneline' shows your commits stacked above where main still sits.

3. Meanwhile a teammate merges an urgent fix into main, so main now has commits your branch does not - the two branches have diverged. You switch back with 'git switch main' and run 'git merge feature/revenue-model'.

4. Because both branches advanced, Git performs a three-way merge: it finds the common ancestor, combines both sets of changes, and - since revenue.sql and the teammate's file did not overlap - creates a merge commit with two parents, joining the histories. main now contains both changes.

5. On a different attempt, both you and the teammate had edited the same lines of pipeline_config.yml. Git cannot choose, so it stops with a CONFLICT message, writes <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers into the file, and 'git status' shows it as 'both modified'. You open the file, keep the correct combined value, delete the markers, run 'git add pipeline_config.yml', then 'git commit' to finish the merge (or 'git merge --abort' to undo the whole attempt and start over).

keyTerminology.meaning: A named, movable pointer to a commit. Because commits record their parents, that pointer effectively names an entire line of history; creating one is cheap and instant.
keyTerminology.importance: Branches are how you isolate feature, experiment, and bugfix work from stable main, and how many engineers work on one repository in parallel without clobbering each other.

keyTerminology.meaning: A special pointer to whatever you currently have checked out - normally the branch you are on (e.g. 'ref: refs/heads/main'), so your working files reflect that branch. In <<<<<<< HEAD conflict markers, HEAD means 'your current branch's version.'
keyTerminology.importance: Knowing where HEAD points tells you which branch new commits will land on and, during a conflict, which side of the markers is yours.

keyTerminology.meaning: A merge where the current branch has no new commits of its own, so Git just moves its pointer forward to the other branch's tip - no merge commit is created and history stays linear.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the simplest, cleanest merge; recognising when you will get one (and when to force '--no-ff' for an explicit merge commit) shapes how your history reads.

keyTerminology.meaning: A merge used when both branches diverged: Git compares the two tips and their common ancestor and writes a new merge commit with two parents, joining the histories.
keyTerminology.importance: It preserves the true branching history and is where merge conflicts can arise when both sides changed the same lines.

keyTerminology.meaning: A situation where two branches changed the same region of a file so Git cannot merge automatically; it inserts markers - <<<<<<< HEAD (your side), ======= (divider), >>>>>>> branch (their side) - and pauses for you to resolve.
keyTerminology.importance: Conflicts are normal and expected in team work; reading the markers and resolving them correctly (then git add + commit) is a core everyday Git skill.

importantConcepts.concept: A branch is a pointer, not a copy of the repo
importantConcepts.explanation: The single most useful mental model is that a branch is just a 41-byte file holding one commit hash. Creating a branch does not duplicate your files, your history, or the .git database - it writes one new reference that points at an existing commit. This is why 'git branch feature' is instantaneous even in a repository with millions of lines of code, and why you should branch freely rather than treating branches as heavyweight. When you commit on a branch, only that branch's pointer moves forward; other branches (like main) stay exactly where they were. Deleting a branch (git branch -d) just removes the pointer - the commits it named still exist as long as another branch or reference can reach them. Internally this is why Git is so fast at branching compared to older tools that literally copied files on the server.

importantConcepts.concept: Fast-forward vs three-way merge, and why merge commits have two parents
importantConcepts.explanation: When you merge, Git first checks whether the branch you are on has diverged from the branch you are merging in. If your branch has no commits the other lacks - it is simply 'behind' - Git can fast-forward: it moves your branch's pointer forward to the other tip, producing a straight, linear history with no extra commit. If instead both branches have their own new commits since they split, Git cannot just slide a pointer; it performs a three-way merge, comparing three snapshots (the common ancestor plus each branch tip) and creating a new merge commit. That merge commit is special because it has two parents - one from each branch - which is exactly what records 'these two lines of history joined here.' You can force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible with 'git merge --no-ff', which many teams do so that every feature integration is visible as a distinct merge in the history.

importantConcepts.concept: Why merge conflicts happen and how to resolve them
importantConcepts.explanation: A merge conflict is not an error or a sign something is broken - it is Git being careful. During a three-way merge, Git compares each side's changes against the common ancestor. If the two branches changed different parts of a file, Git merges them automatically. But if both branches changed the same lines (or one deleted a file the other edited), Git cannot know which version is correct, so rather than silently discarding someone's work it stops and asks you. It rewrites the conflicted file to show both versions between markers: your branch's content sits between '<<<<<<< HEAD' and '=======', and the incoming branch's content sits between '=======' and '>>>>>>> branchname'. You resolve it by opening the file, deciding on the final content (keep one side, keep the other, or combine them), deleting all three marker lines, then running 'git add <file>' to tell Git it is resolved, and finally 'git commit' (or 'git merge --continue'). 'git status' lists every conflicted file, and 'git merge --abort' cleanly undoes the whole merge if you want to start over.

importantConcepts.concept: Rebase vs merge, and the golden rule
importantConcepts.explanation: Merging and rebasing both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they shape history differently. 'git merge' preserves what actually happened: it keeps both branches' commits and joins them with a merge commit, so the history shows the true parallel work. 'git rebase' instead rewrites history to be linear: it takes your branch's commits and replays them one by one on top of the target branch's latest commit, as if you had started your work from there. Rebasing gives a clean, straight line that is easy to read, but because it creates new commits (new hashes) in place of the originals, it changes history. That leads to the golden rule of rebasing: never rebase commits that have already been pushed and shared, because rewriting shared history forces everyone else to reconcile diverging copies and can lose work. Rebase private, local, unpushed branches to tidy them up; merge (or use pull requests) when integrating shared branches into main.

variationsAndTypes: **Fast-forward merge:** the current branch has not diverged, so Git just advances its pointer to the incoming tip - linear history, no merge commit; disable with '--no-ff' to force one.
**Three-way (true) merge:** both branches have new commits, so Git builds a merge commit with two parents from the two tips and their common ancestor; this is where conflicts can appear.

**Rebase (linear integration):** replays your commits on top of another branch to produce a straight history instead of a merge commit - great for private branches, dangerous on shared/pushed ones (the golden rule).

**Branching strategies:** feature branches (one branch per task), GitFlow (long-lived develop/release/hotfix branches), and trunk-based development (tiny, short-lived branches merged into main constantly).

**Short-lived vs long-lived branches:** short-lived branches merge back within hours or days to minimise divergence and conflicts; long-lived branches (release, develop) live for weeks and need periodic syncing with main.
advantages: **Isolation:** feature, experiment, and bugfix work happens on its own branch, so unfinished or broken changes never destabilise the deployable main branch.
**Cheap and fast:** a branch is just a pointer, so creating, switching, and deleting branches is instant and costs almost no disk space - branch freely.
**Parallel collaboration:** many engineers work on the same repository simultaneously on separate branches, then converge safely through merges and pull-request review.
**Traceable history:** merge commits (and pull requests) record when and how each line of work was integrated, so you can see and, if needed, revert exactly which change entered main.
**Safe experimentation:** you can try a risky refactor on a branch and simply delete it if it does not work out, with zero impact on main.
disadvantages: **Merge conflicts:** when two branches touch the same lines, someone must resolve the conflict by hand, which takes time and, if done carelessly, can drop changes.
**Divergence over time:** long-lived branches drift far from main, making eventual merges large, painful, and conflict-prone ('merge hell').
**History can get messy:** many merge commits and criss-crossing branches make 'git log' hard to read unless the team agrees on a strategy.
**Rebase footguns:** rebasing shared or pushed branches rewrites history and can force teammates into painful recovery or lost work if the golden rule is ignored.
**Process overhead:** branching strategies, pull-request reviews, and CI gates add coordination cost that can slow very small teams if applied too heavily.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use a branch for any change you would not commit straight to main: a new dbt model, an Airflow DAG, a bugfix, or an experiment. Use merge (often via a pull request) to integrate reviewed work into main and to preserve real history. Force '--no-ff' when you want every feature to appear as a distinct merge. Use rebase only on your own private, unpushed branch to tidy commits before opening a PR.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid committing risky or unreviewed work directly to main. Avoid long-lived branches that drift far from main - sync frequently to prevent 'merge hell'. Never rebase branches you have already pushed and shared. Avoid resolving a conflict by blindly accepting one side without understanding both changes, and avoid heavyweight branching strategies for a tiny solo project where they add pure overhead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a shared cookbook the whole kitchen relies on - that trusted master copy is 'main'. You want to invent a new sauce recipe, but you must not scribble in the master cookbook while service is running. So you photocopy nothing; instead you take a bookmark, label it 'new-sauce', and clip it to the current page - that is a branch (just a pointer, not a whole new cookbook). You draft your recipe on your own pages that only your bookmark tracks. When it is perfected, you 'merge' it into the master book. If nobody edited the master meanwhile, you simply slide the master bookmark to include your pages (a fast-forward). If a colleague also added recipes, an editor stitches both sets in and adds a note 'merged new-sauce and new-dessert here' (a merge commit with two parents). The headache comes if you and your colleague both rewrote the exact same soup recipe on the same line: the editor cannot guess whose is right, so they lay both versions side by side with markers and ask you to decide the final wording before the master book is updated - that is a merge conflict.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Creating a branch makes a full copy of the repository, so branches are expensive.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A branch is just a tiny pointer to a commit - a 41-byte file holding one hash. Creating it copies nothing and is instant, even in huge repos. That is exactly why Git encourages branching liberally; only the pointer moves as you commit, and deleting a branch removes only the pointer.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A merge conflict means something is broken or I did something wrong.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Conflicts are a normal, expected part of collaborating. They simply mean two branches changed the same lines and Git is refusing to guess, so it asks you to decide. Resolving one - editing the file, removing the markers, git add, then commit - is routine everyday work, not an error to fear.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rebasing is always better than merging because it gives cleaner history.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Rebase does produce a tidy linear history, but it rewrites commits (new hashes), which is dangerous on branches you have already pushed and shared - the golden rule says never do that. Merge preserves true history and is safe for shared branches. Use rebase for private local cleanup, merge for integrating shared work; neither is universally 'better'.

productionConsiderations.scalability: As team and repo size grow, prefer short-lived branches and frequent merges to main so branches never drift far apart; large teams often adopt trunk-based development with feature flags so many engineers integrate small changes daily instead of maintaining big long-lived branches that conflict.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Keep main always deployable by only merging branches that passed CI (tests, linting, dbt build/compile) and code review via pull requests; protect main with branch-protection rules so nothing merges unreviewed or with failing checks.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because merges are recorded as commits, a bad merge can be reverted cleanly ('git revert' the merge commit), and branches let you isolate and roll back a change without disturbing unrelated work; never force-push to shared branches so history other people rely on stays intact.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track branch health: how far each branch is ahead/behind main, how long branches live before merging, and how often conflicts occur - long-lived, far-behind branches are a leading indicator of painful merges and should be flagged and rebased/merged promptly.
productionConsiderations.security: Protect the default branch with required reviews and status checks, restrict who can push or force-push, sign commits or require verified signatures where compliance demands it, and never commit secrets on any branch since history is shared and hard to fully erase.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Catching conflicts and defects on a branch during review is far cheaper than in production; short-lived branches reduce the expensive rework of resolving huge divergent merges, and deleting merged branches keeps the repo tidy and CI focused only on active work.
productionConsiderations.performance: Git branching itself is effectively free, but very large repositories benefit from shallow clones, sparse-checkout, and pruning stale branches; keeping branches short-lived also keeps merges small and fast to compute and review.

codeExamples.title: Create a feature branch, commit, and fast-forward merge back to main
codeExamples.overview: Branch off main to build a new pipeline model, make commits in isolation, then merge back with a fast-forward (and see how --no-ff would differ).
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Confirm where you are and list branches (* marks the current one)
git branch

# 2) Create a feature branch AND switch to it in one step
git switch -c feature/revenue-model
#    older equivalent: git checkout -b feature/revenue-model

# 3) Do the work: create a new dbt/SQL model file and commit it
echo 'select customer_id, sum(amount) as revenue from orders group by 1' > models/revenue.sql
git add models/revenue.sql
git commit -m "Add revenue model"

# 4) See the shape of history so far
git log --graph --oneline --all

# 5) Switch back to the stable branch
git switch main

# 6) Merge the feature in. main has NOT moved, so this fast-forwards
git merge feature/revenue-model

# 7) (Alternative) force an explicit merge commit even when FF is possible
#    git merge --no-ff feature/revenue-model

# 8) Delete the merged branch pointer - the commits stay in main
git branch -d feature/revenue-model
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git branch' lists local branches and stars the current one. 'git switch -c feature/revenue-model' creates a new pointer at main's commit and moves HEAD onto it, so subsequent commits land on the feature branch. After adding models/revenue.sql and committing, only the feature pointer advances - main is untouched. 'git log --graph --oneline --all' draws the history. Switching back to main and running 'git merge feature/revenue-model' fast-forwards because main has no commits of its own; Git simply slides main's pointer to the feature tip (no merge commit). '--no-ff' would instead create a merge commit to record the integration explicitly. 'git branch -d' deletes the now-merged branch pointer safely.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git branch
* main
$ git switch -c feature/revenue-model
Switched to a new branch 'feature/revenue-model'
$ git commit -m "Add revenue model"
[feature/revenue-model 3a9f1c2] Add revenue model
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 models/revenue.sql
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git merge feature/revenue-model
Updating 8d2e4b1..3a9f1c2
Fast-forward
 models/revenue.sql | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git branch -d feature/revenue-model
Deleted branch feature/revenue-model (was 3a9f1c2).
codeExamples.commonIssues: 'git branch -d' refuses to delete a branch whose commits are not yet merged (use -D to force, but only if you truly want to discard that work). Committing while still on main defeats the purpose of the feature branch - always switch first. A fast-forward leaves no merge commit, so if your team wants every feature visible in history, use '--no-ff'. Forgetting 'git add' before commit means your new file is not included.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use a clear branch naming convention like 'feature/', 'bugfix/', 'hotfix/' so branches are self-describing in 'git branch'. Run 'git switch -' to jump back to the previous branch quickly. Configure 'git config --global merge.ff false' (or per-repo) if your team prefers explicit merge commits for every feature.

codeExamples.title: Three-way merge that creates a merge commit (both branches diverged)
codeExamples.overview: Simulate two branches each gaining new commits, then merge to produce a merge commit with two parents, inspecting history before and after.
codeExamples.code:
# Setup: main and a feature branch that will BOTH get new commits
git switch -c feature/add-dag
echo 'dag = DAG("daily_load")' > dags/daily_load.py
git add dags/daily_load.py
git commit -m "Add daily_load DAG"

# Meanwhile, main also moves forward (a teammate's fix)
git switch main
echo '# hotfix: bump timeout' >> config/settings.py
git add config/settings.py
git commit -m "Hotfix: bump timeout"

# History BEFORE the merge - two diverged lines
git log --graph --oneline --all

# Merge the feature into main -> three-way merge, makes a merge commit
git merge feature/add-dag
#    Git opens an editor for the merge commit message; save to accept it

# History AFTER the merge - the two lines join at a merge commit
git log --graph --oneline --all

# Inspect the merge commit: note it has TWO parents
git show --no-patch --format='%h parents: %p' HEAD
codeExamples.breakdown: First a feature branch gets a commit (the new DAG). Then, back on main, a separate commit lands (the hotfix), so the two branches have each moved forward from their common ancestor - they have diverged. 'git log --graph --oneline --all' before the merge shows two separate lines. 'git merge feature/add-dag' now cannot fast-forward; Git performs a three-way merge using the merge base plus both tips, and because the two files differ it merges cleanly into a new merge commit (Git opens an editor for its message). The 'after' log shows the two lines converging at that merge commit. 'git show --no-patch --format=...' prints the merge commit's two parent hashes, proving it joins both histories.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
# before the merge:
* 7c1a9e0 (main) Hotfix: bump timeout
| * 4b8d3f2 (feature/add-dag) Add daily_load DAG
|/
* 8d2e4b1 Initial pipeline

$ git merge feature/add-dag
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 dags/daily_load.py | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 dags/daily_load.py

# after the merge:
*   e5f0a71 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'feature/add-dag'
|\
| * 4b8d3f2 (feature/add-dag) Add daily_load DAG
* | 7c1a9e0 Hotfix: bump timeout
|/
* 8d2e4b1 Initial pipeline

$ git show --no-patch --format='%h parents: %p' HEAD
e5f0a71 parents: 7c1a9e0 4b8d3f2
codeExamples.commonIssues: If the two branches happened to touch the same lines you would get a conflict instead of a clean merge commit (see the next example). Some teams dislike the extra merge commits a three-way merge creates and prefer rebase for a linear history. Aborting the editor without saving the merge message cancels the merge on some configs, so save and exit. 'git log' without '--all' hides branches you are not on, which can make the diverged shape confusing.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add a git alias for graph logs: 'git config --global alias.lg "log --graph --oneline --all --decorate"'. Keep feature branches short-lived and merge often so three-way merges stay small. Use 'git merge --log' to include the merged commits' summaries in the merge commit message for a clearer audit trail.

codeExamples.title: Induce and resolve a merge conflict (two branches edit the same lines)
codeExamples.overview: Two branches change the same lines of a shared pipeline config, causing a conflict; read the markers, resolve by editing, then stage and commit - and see how to abort instead.
codeExamples.code:
# On main, the config has: schedule = "@daily"
# Branch A changes it to hourly
git switch -c feature/hourly
sed -i 's/@daily/@hourly/' config/pipeline.yml
git commit -am "Run pipeline hourly"

# Back on main, someone else changes the SAME line to weekly
git switch main
sed -i 's/@daily/@weekly/' config/pipeline.yml
git commit -am "Run pipeline weekly"

# Merge the feature -> CONFLICT on the same line
git merge feature/hourly

# See which files conflicted
git status

# Look at the conflict markers Git wrote into the file
cat config/pipeline.yml
#   <<<<<<< HEAD
#   schedule = "@weekly"
#   =======
#   schedule = "@hourly"
#   >>>>>>> feature/hourly

# Resolve: edit the file to the final desired value, removing ALL markers
printf 'schedule = "@hourly"\n' > config/pipeline.yml

# Stage the resolved file and complete the merge
git add config/pipeline.yml
git commit -m "Merge feature/hourly: settle on hourly schedule"

# --- If instead you want to back out entirely, before committing: ---
# git merge --abort        # restores the pre-merge state, no changes kept
codeExamples.breakdown: Branch 'feature/hourly' changes the schedule line to @hourly; main independently changes the same line to @weekly. When you 'git merge feature/hourly', Git compares both sides against the common ancestor, sees the same line changed two ways, and cannot decide - so it writes conflict markers and pauses. 'git status' lists the file as 'both modified'. Inside config/pipeline.yml, the content between '<<<<<<< HEAD' and '=======' is main's version (@weekly, because HEAD is main), and the content between '=======' and '>>>>>>> feature/hourly' is the incoming branch's version (@hourly). You resolve by editing the file to the final content you want and deleting all three marker lines, then 'git add' to mark it resolved and 'git commit' to write the merge commit. 'git merge --abort' would instead discard the in-progress merge and restore the state from before you ran git merge.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git merge feature/hourly
Auto-merging config/pipeline.yml
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config/pipeline.yml
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

$ git status
On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
	both modified:   config/pipeline.yml

$ cat config/pipeline.yml
<<<<<<< HEAD
schedule = "@weekly"
=======
schedule = "@hourly"
>>>>>>> feature/hourly

$ git add config/pipeline.yml
$ git commit -m "Merge feature/hourly: settle on hourly schedule"
[main 9d4c2a8] Merge feature/hourly: settle on hourly schedule
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to delete the marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) leaves them in the file, which breaks the config and often the build - always remove all three. Running 'git commit' before 'git add' on the resolved file leaves the merge incomplete. Blindly keeping one side without reading the other can silently drop a needed change. If many files conflict and you are unsure, 'git merge --abort' cleanly resets so you can retry after syncing.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'git diff' during a conflict to see the combined diff, or 'git checkout --ours/--theirs <file>' when you truly want one whole side. 'git mergetool' opens a configured visual merge tool for tricky conflicts. To reduce conflicts, merge or rebase main into long-lived branches frequently so divergence stays small, and keep unrelated changes in separate small branches.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: Two data engineers must add features to the same analytics repository at the same time - one adding a new revenue dbt model, the other tweaking the shared pipeline schedule - without breaking the main branch that CI/CD deploys to production. They need isolation, a review gate before anything reaches main, and a safe way to handle the conflict that arises when both touch the same config.
endToEndExample.inputData: A Git repository with a protected 'main' branch (deployed by CI), a dbt/SQL project under models/, Airflow DAGs under dags/, and a shared config/pipeline.yml. Two engineers each start from the same main commit.
endToEndExample.architecture: Each engineer creates a short-lived feature branch off main with 'git switch -c'. They commit in isolation, push, and open pull requests. CI runs tests and 'dbt build' on each branch. main is protected: merges require a passing build and a review. When the second PR conflicts with the first (both edited pipeline.yml), the engineer syncs main into their branch, resolves the conflict locally (edit, git add, commit), and only then merges. Merges into main use '--no-ff' (via the PR) so every feature is a distinct merge commit for traceability.
processingSteps: 1. Engineer A: 'git switch -c feature/revenue-model', adds models/revenue.sql, commits, pushes, and opens a pull request; CI runs dbt build on the branch, it passes, a reviewer approves.
2. Engineer B: from the same starting main, 'git switch -c feature/hourly-schedule', edits config/pipeline.yml to change the schedule, commits, pushes, and opens a pull request in parallel.
3. Engineer A's PR is reviewed and merged into main first (a clean three-way merge commit); main now contains the revenue model and any earlier hotfixes.

4. Engineer B's PR now conflicts because main's pipeline.yml changed on the same lines: B runs 'git switch feature/hourly-schedule', then 'git merge main' (or rebase) to bring main in, and Git reports CONFLICT in config/pipeline.yml.

5. B inspects with 'git status' and 'git diff', opens pipeline.yml, sees the <<<<<<< HEAD / ======= / >>>>>>> markers, edits to the correct combined schedule, deletes the markers, runs 'git add config/pipeline.yml' and 'git commit' to finish the merge; if it had gone wrong, 'git merge --abort' would have reset cleanly.

6. With the conflict resolved and CI green again, B's pull request is merged into main via a reviewed '--no-ff' merge; both features are now in main, each visible as its own merge commit, and both feature branches are deleted.
endToEndExample.output: A main branch that contains both engineers' features, stayed deployable throughout, and records each integration as a distinct merge commit. The conflicting config ends with the correct agreed value, and no work was lost.
endToEndExample.monitoring: CI status checks on every branch and PR (tests, dbt build/compile), branch-protection rules that block merging on failure or without review, and 'git log --graph' plus the PR history showing exactly when and how each feature merged.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The conflict is handled by resolving locally (edit + git add + commit) with 'git merge --abort' as the escape hatch; a bad merge that slips through can be undone by reverting the merge commit ('git revert -m 1 <merge>'); branch protection prevents unreviewed or failing changes from ever reaching main.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Two engineers shipped overlapping changes in parallel without destabilising production: branches isolated their work, pull requests gated it, a three-way merge integrated the non-conflicting file automatically, and the one true conflict on the shared config was resolved deliberately by a human - exactly the everyday workflow branching and merging exist to support.

industryUseCases.company: Analytics teams using dbt with pull-request review
industryUseCases.problem: Many analysts edit models in the same dbt repo; without isolation, half-finished or broken SQL would reach the deployed main branch and corrupt dashboards.
industryUseCases.solution: Each change goes on a short-lived feature branch, gets a pull request where CI runs 'dbt build' and a peer reviews it, and only merges into a protected main after passing - with conflicts on shared models resolved locally before merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: main stays deployable, changes are reviewed and traceable, and parallel work by many analysts converges safely instead of clobbering a single shared copy.

industryUseCases.company: Platform teams managing Airflow DAGs and infrastructure-as-code
industryUseCases.problem: Multiple engineers modify DAGs and Terraform in one repo simultaneously, frequently touching shared config files and causing merge conflicts.
industryUseCases.solution: Feature branches per change, frequent syncing of main into branches to keep divergence small, and disciplined conflict resolution (git status, edit, git add, commit) plus branch protection requiring green CI before merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fewer painful 'merge hell' situations, conflicts caught and resolved on branches rather than in production, and a clean audit trail of who changed which DAG when.

industryUseCases.company: High-throughput product teams using trunk-based development
industryUseCases.problem: A large team needed to integrate many changes per day, but long-lived branches drifted far from main and produced huge, conflict-ridden merges.
industryUseCases.solution: Adopt trunk-based development: tiny, short-lived branches merged into main multiple times a day behind feature flags, with fast CI and small pull requests to minimise divergence.
industryUseCases.benefits: Conflicts stay small and rare because branches barely diverge, integration is continuous, and main is always releasable - enabling rapid, safe deployment at scale.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Branching itself is effectively free, so scale comes from process: prefer short-lived branches and frequent merges (or trunk-based development with feature flags) so branches never drift far from main; large monorepos add shallow clones, sparse-checkout, and automatic pruning of stale branches to keep operations fast.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Branches isolate risk so a broken change never reaches main; because every integration is a commit, a bad merge can be reverted cleanly ('git revert -m 1 <merge commit>'), and Git's reflog can recover commits after a mistaken reset or hard branch delete - never force-push shared branches so recovery stays possible.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Keep main continuously deployable by gating every merge behind passing CI and review; with trunk-based flows and feature flags, incomplete work can sit merged-but-disabled in main, so releases never wait on a long-lived branch to finish.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: The remote (e.g. GitHub) plus every developer's clone are full copies of history, so the repository is inherently backed up; protect the default branch, keep tags/releases immutable, and rely on the reflog and unmerged branch commits to recover from accidental deletions or bad merges.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Small, frequent merges compute and review faster than giant divergent ones; use '--no-ff' or squash-merge deliberately per team convention, keep branches short-lived, and prune merged branches so CI and tooling only track active work.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Resolving conflicts and catching defects on a branch during review is dramatically cheaper than fixing a production pipeline that shipped bad data; short-lived branches cut the expensive rework of large merges, and deleting merged branches trims CI runs and storage overhead.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Protect the default branch with required reviews and status checks, restrict who can push or force-push, require signed/verified commits where compliance demands, and never commit secrets on any branch since shared history is hard to fully purge (needs history-rewriting tools and force-push coordination).
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track how far branches are ahead/behind main, branch age before merge, PR review time, and conflict frequency; long-lived, far-behind branches are the leading indicator of painful merges, and a clear 'git log --graph' plus PR history gives an auditable record of every integration.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Gate merges to main on CI that runs the pipeline's tests and 'dbt build'/compile so only changes that pass validation reach production; after resolving a conflict in transformation logic, re-run tests to confirm the merged result is correct and not a half-applied change.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Rely on commit and merge history as the primary audit log (who merged what, when, and via which PR), alert on force-pushes to protected branches and on failing merges/CI, and record the resolution decision in the merge commit message so future readers understand why a conflict was settled a given way.

recommendedPractices: **Branch for every change:** never commit unreviewed or risky work straight to main - create a feature/bugfix branch, then merge via a pull request after review and green CI.
**Keep branches short-lived:** merge back within hours or a few days and sync main into your branch frequently so divergence - and therefore conflicts - stays small.

**Read both sides before resolving a conflict:** understand what HEAD and the incoming branch each changed, choose or combine deliberately, and remove every <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> marker before staging.
**Protect main:** require passing CI and review to merge, and never force-push shared branches so history other people rely on stays intact.
**Rebase only private branches:** tidy your own unpushed commits with rebase, but merge (never rebase) branches that are already shared - the golden rule.
engineeringStandards: Gate every merge into main on automated checks (tests, linting, dbt build/compile) so only validated changes reach the deployable branch.
Delete branches promptly after they merge so the branch list reflects only active work and stale pointers do not accumulate.
Prefer small, focused branches and pull requests over large ones, so reviews are meaningful and merges stay easy to reason about.
designRecommendations: Pick one branching strategy for the team (feature branches, GitFlow, or trunk-based) and apply it consistently rather than mixing conventions.
Decide as a team on fast-forward vs '--no-ff' (or squash) merges so history reads consistently and every feature integration is traceable.
Keep unrelated changes on separate branches so a conflict or revert in one does not entangle the other.
namingConventions: Prefix branches by intent and scope, e.g. 'feature/revenue-model', 'bugfix/null-customer-key', 'hotfix/timeout' so 'git branch' is self-describing.
Use lowercase, hyphenated, ticket-referencing names (e.g. 'feature/DATA-123-add-dag') to link branches to work items.
Reserve protected, meaningful names for long-lived branches (main, develop, release/*) and never repurpose them for ad-hoc work.
documentationStandards: Write clear commit and merge messages, and in a merge that resolved a conflict, note in the message how and why the conflict was settled.
Document the team's branching strategy and merge policy (FF vs no-ff, who can merge to main) in the repository's CONTRIBUTING guide.
Record branch-protection and review requirements so new contributors know the workflow before opening a pull request.
testingStrategies: Run the full test suite / dbt build on each branch and pull request so conflicts and defects are caught before merging to main.
After resolving a merge conflict, re-run tests to confirm the merged code actually works - resolution can introduce logically wrong combinations.
Test that main stays deployable by running CI on the post-merge commit, not just the branch, so merge commits themselves are validated.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) in the file after 'resolving' a conflict.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: In a hurry, an engineer keeps the desired text but forgets to delete the three marker lines Git inserted, or resolves several files and misses one.
commonMistakes.impact: The file becomes invalid - a YAML config, SQL model, or Python DAG with stray marker lines breaks the build or, worse, silently misbehaves in production.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: After editing to the final content, delete every marker line, then run 'git status' and 'git diff' to confirm no markers remain (grep for '<<<<<<<' across files), before 'git add' and commit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting a feature branch live for weeks without syncing main into it.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels safer to keep working undisturbed, and pulling in main's changes seems like an interruption, so the branch drifts further and further from main.
commonMistakes.impact: The eventual merge is enormous and conflict-ridden ('merge hell'), risky to resolve, and hard to review - exactly the situation branching was meant to avoid.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Keep branches short-lived and merge or rebase main into your branch frequently so divergence stays small and conflicts are tiny and manageable when they do occur.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rebasing a branch that has already been pushed and shared with teammates.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Rebase produces a tidy linear history, and tutorials often praise it, so engineers reach for it without realising it rewrites commit hashes on shared branches.
commonMistakes.impact: Everyone who had the old commits now has diverging history; pulls fail or create duplicate commits, and careless force-pushes can overwrite or lose teammates' work.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Follow the golden rule: rebase only private, unpushed branches to clean them up locally; for shared branches use merge (or open a pull request) and never force-push shared history.

comparisonSection.optionA: git merge (three-way merge with a merge commit)
comparisonSection.optionB: git rebase (replay commits for a linear history)
comparisonSection.explanation: Merge preserves true history: it keeps both branches' commits and joins them with a merge commit that has two parents, so you can see the parallel work exactly as it happened - safe for shared branches. Rebase rewrites your branch's commits onto the tip of another branch to produce a clean straight line, which reads more simply but changes commit hashes; because of that it must never be used on branches already pushed and shared (the golden rule). Use rebase for private cleanup, merge for integrating shared work.

A fast-forward happens when the branch you are on has no new commits of its own, so Git just slides its pointer forward to the incoming tip - history stays linear and no merge commit is made. A three-way merge happens when both branches diverged, so Git builds a merge commit with two parents from the two tips and their common ancestor. Fast-forwards are cleaner but leave no record that a feature was integrated; teams that want that record force a merge commit with '--no-ff'.

comparisonSection.optionB: Trunk-based development (tiny short-lived branches into main)
comparisonSection.explanation: GitFlow uses several long-lived branches and a defined promotion path, which suits scheduled releases and versioned products but tends to produce large, conflict-prone merges and more overhead. Trunk-based development keeps branches tiny and short-lived, merging into main many times a day (often behind feature flags), which minimises divergence and conflicts and keeps main continuously deployable - favoured by high-throughput teams and CI/CD-driven data platforms, at the cost of requiring strong automated testing.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a Git branch, and why is creating one cheap?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A branch is a named, movable pointer to a commit - essentially a tiny file holding one commit hash. Because commits record their parents, that pointer names a whole line of history. Creating a branch is cheap and instant because it copies nothing; it just writes a new pointer at an existing commit. As you commit on the branch, only that pointer moves forward.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the core mental model: branch = pointer, not a copy. Mentioning the tiny ref file and that only the pointer moves shows you understand why Git branching is so fast compared to older tools.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is HEAD, and how do you create and switch to a new branch?
beginnerQuestions.answer: HEAD is a pointer to what you currently have checked out - normally the branch you are on, so your working files reflect it. You create and switch in one step with 'git switch -c feature/x' (or the older 'git checkout -b feature/x'); 'git switch main' moves back, and 'git branch' lists branches with '*' marking the current one. Deleting a merged branch is 'git branch -d name'.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: They want you to connect HEAD (where you are) with the create/switch commands. Naming both the modern 'switch' and older 'checkout' forms demonstrates practical, current knowledge.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between a fast-forward merge and a three-way merge?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A fast-forward merge happens when the branch you are on has no commits the other lacks, so Git just moves your branch's pointer forward to the incoming tip - no merge commit, linear history. A three-way merge happens when both branches diverged (each has new commits); Git compares both tips against their common ancestor and creates a merge commit with two parents joining the histories. You can force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible with 'git merge --no-ff'.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key is recognising divergence: no divergence -> fast-forward; both moved -> merge commit with two parents. Mentioning --no-ff shows awareness of history-style choices teams make.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why do merge conflicts happen, and how do you resolve one?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A conflict happens when both branches changed the same region of a file (or one deleted a file the other edited), so Git cannot decide automatically and refuses to guess. It writes markers into the file - your side between '<<<<<<< HEAD' and '=======', the incoming side between '=======' and '>>>>>>> branch' - and pauses. You resolve by editing the file to the final content, deleting all markers, running 'git add <file>' to mark it resolved, then 'git commit' (or 'git merge --continue'). 'git status' lists conflicted files and 'git merge --abort' backs out entirely.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want the cause (same lines changed), that conflicts are normal not errors, and the exact resolution workflow including add + commit and the abort escape hatch.

advancedQuestions.question: When would you use rebase instead of merge, and what is the golden rule of rebasing?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use rebase to produce a clean linear history by replaying your branch's commits on top of another branch - ideal for tidying your own private, unpushed commits before opening a pull request. Use merge to integrate shared work, since it preserves true history with a merge commit. The golden rule is: never rebase commits that have already been pushed and shared, because rebasing rewrites commit hashes and forces everyone else into diverging history, which breaks pulls and risks losing work. Rebase local/private, merge shared.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests judgement, not just mechanics. The strong answer contrasts linear-vs-preserved history, ties rebase's danger to rewritten hashes, and states the golden rule explicitly.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you keep main always deployable when many engineers work in parallel, and how do you recover from a bad merge?
advancedQuestions.answer: Keep every change on a short-lived branch, gate merges to main behind passing CI (tests, dbt build) and code review via pull requests, and protect main so nothing merges unreviewed or with failing checks; trunk-based development with feature flags lets incomplete work sit merged-but-disabled. If a bad merge still reaches main, revert it cleanly with 'git revert -m 1 <merge commit>' (the -m 1 keeps main's first-parent line), and use the reflog to recover commits after an accidental reset or hard delete. Never force-push shared branches so recovery stays possible.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This checks production maturity: branch protection + CI + review to keep main good, revert of a merge commit (including the -m parent selection), and reflog for recovery. Bonus for feature flags and no force-push.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You and a teammate both edited the same lines of a shared pipeline config on separate branches. Your teammate's branch merged into main first. Now your merge fails with a conflict. Walk through how you safely finish your merge.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: First understand the situation: main advanced with the teammate's change to the same lines I changed, so a three-way merge cannot auto-resolve. I should bring main into my branch and resolve locally rather than on main. I'll run git status to see which files conflict, open each, read both sides of the markers (HEAD is my current branch, the incoming side is main/theirs), and decide the correct combined value - not blindly pick a side. After editing and removing all markers, I stage each resolved file and complete the merge, then re-run tests before merging to main. If it gets messy I can abort and retry.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Switch to my branch and merge main into it ('git switch feature/mine' then 'git merge main'), which triggers the conflict. Run 'git status' to list the 'both modified' files and 'git diff' to see the conflict. Open each conflicted file, read the content between '<<<<<<< HEAD' (my side) and '=======' and between '=======' and '>>>>>>> main' (their side), edit to the correct final content, and delete all marker lines. 'git add' each resolved file, then 'git commit' to finish the merge. Re-run CI/tests to confirm the merged result is correct, then merge my branch into main via the reviewed PR. If anything goes wrong mid-resolution, 'git merge --abort' resets cleanly so I can retry.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a branching and merging workflow for a data engineering team of 20 engineers working in one dbt + Airflow repository, so main is always deployable, work happens in parallel, and conflicts are manageable.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use short-lived feature branches off a protected main, one per change, named by intent (feature/, bugfix/, hotfix/). Every change goes through a pull request with required CI (tests, dbt build/compile) and at least one review before merge. Encourage frequent syncing of main into branches (or rebase of private branches) to keep divergence small. Merge to main with a consistent policy (squash or --no-ff) so history is clean and each feature is traceable, and delete branches after merge. For high throughput, lean toward trunk-based development with feature flags so incomplete work can merge disabled.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: GitFlow's long-lived branches suit versioned releases but cause big conflict-prone merges; trunk-based needs strong automated testing but keeps conflicts tiny and main always releasable. Fast-forward/squash merges give clean history but hide the branch shape; --no-ff records every integration at the cost of more merge commits. Branch protection and required review add process overhead but are what keep main trustworthy at 20-engineer scale.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: As the team grows, shorten branch lifetimes further, add faster/parallel CI so review gates do not bottleneck, adopt feature flags for trunk-based flow, prune stale branches automatically, and monitor branch age and conflict frequency; for a growing monorepo use shallow clones and sparse-checkout so client-side Git operations stay fast.

followUpQuestions: What exactly do the <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, and >>>>>>> branch markers each delimit during a conflict?
How does 'git merge --abort' differ from resolving a conflict, and when would you use it?
What does 'git branch -d' do versus 'git branch -D', and when is each safe?
How would you revert a change that was introduced by a merge commit rather than a normal commit?
Why is the golden rule 'never rebase shared/pushed branches', and what breaks if you ignore it?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A branch is a cheap, movable pointer to a commit that isolates work from main; merging integrates branches - a fast-forward just moves the pointer, a three-way merge makes a merge commit with two parents, and overlapping edits cause a conflict you resolve by editing, git add, then commit.
keyConcepts: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit, not a copy of the repo; creating one is instant.
HEAD points to your current branch; new commits advance that branch's pointer.
Fast-forward merge just moves the pointer forward; a three-way merge builds a merge commit with two parents.
A conflict means both branches changed the same lines; Git writes <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers and pauses.
Resolve a conflict by editing to the final content, removing markers, 'git add', then 'git commit' (or 'git merge --abort' to back out).
commands: git switch -c feature/x                 # create + switch (old: git checkout -b feature/x)
git merge feature/x                     # merge into current branch (add --no-ff to force a merge commit)
git status                              # during a conflict, shows 'both modified' files
git add pipeline.yml && git commit      # mark conflict resolved and finish the merge
git merge --abort                       # cancel an in-progress merge and restore prior state
interviewPoints: A branch is a pointer, not a copy - that is why branching is cheap and instant.
No divergence -> fast-forward; both branches moved -> three-way merge commit with two parents.
Conflicts are normal: same lines changed on both sides; resolve with edit + git add + commit.
Golden rule: never rebase shared/pushed branches - rebase private, merge shared.
Keep main deployable via short-lived branches, PR review, and passing CI before merge.
quickNotes: In conflict markers, <<<<<<< HEAD is YOUR side; >>>>>>> branch is the INCOMING side.
Always delete all three marker lines; grep for '<<<<<<<' before committing.
'git branch -d' only deletes merged branches; '-D' force-deletes (may lose work).
Keep branches short-lived and sync main often to avoid conflict-heavy 'merge hell'.
Revert a merge commit with 'git revert -m 1 <merge>'; use the reflog to recover mistakes.

keyTakeaways: A Git branch is a cheap, movable pointer to a commit - not a copy of the repository - so branching is instant; you create/switch with 'git switch -c', track where you are via HEAD, and use branches to isolate feature, bugfix, and experimental work from a stable, deployable main.

Merging integrates one branch into another: a fast-forward simply moves the current branch's pointer forward when it has not diverged, while a three-way merge builds a merge commit with two parents when both branches have new commits, preserving the true branching history.

Merge conflicts are normal, not errors: they happen when two branches change the same lines, and Git pauses and writes <<<<<<< HEAD / ======= / >>>>>>> branch markers; you resolve by editing to the final content, deleting every marker, running 'git add', then 'git commit' - or 'git merge --abort' to back out.

Rebase replays commits for a clean linear history while merge preserves history with a merge commit; the golden rule is to rebase only private, unpushed branches and never rebase shared/pushed ones, choosing merge (or pull requests) to integrate shared work safely.

In real data engineering workflows, keep main always deployable by developing on short-lived feature branches, syncing frequently to avoid 'merge hell', gating merges behind passing CI and pull-request review, and picking a consistent branching strategy (feature branches, GitFlow, or trunk-based development).
